audio.notes: Public domain in the United States: the recording was first published before 1926 (Music Modernization Act schedule, as of 2026) and the composition before 1931 or is traditional. The qasida is on a classical Arabic poem. Transfer by the Internet Archive's Great 78 Project from a George Blood digitisation; no licence claim on the item.

object.medium: Acoustic 78 rpm gramophone recording; a qasida with takht
object.description: The most popular singer in Egypt in the first decade of the century, in a form the gramophone could barely hold. 'Abd al-Hayy Hilmi was the wild one of the Nahda, a drinker and a genius, who would stop a performance when the mood left him and sing for an hour when it came; he died at fifty-five in 1912. The qasida is the oldest Arab song form, a classical poem sung line by line with the singer improvising on each, and here he has behind him the violin of Sami al-Shawwa, 'the prince of the violin', then at the start of a career that lasted into the age of Umm Kulthum. The side was cut in Cairo around 1909 and pressed a decade later in New York for the Arab communities of the Americas. The label stands in for a portrait.
facts: Opera Disc of New York reissued the Gramophone Company's Arab masters without licence in the early 1920s; it is why many survive.
Sami al-Shawwa (1885-1965) later accompanied Umm Kulthum and toured the Americas.
The Nahda singers' improvisation, the layali and mawwal, is the ancestor of the long tarab performances of the mid-century.
